title: Latin America
hookLine: base communities reading the Bible together, and a Pentecostal wave
carry: the bible read by the poor

lines: A TIN ROOF, A GOSPEL, A QUESTION.
cards: A village chapel with a tin roof. The Gospel has just been read: Jesus feeding a hungry crowd. Instead of a sermon, a question goes around the benches.
What do you hear? A fisherman says the crowd was hungry because somebody kept the bread. A grandmother says the disciples wanted to send people away, and Jesus said no, you feed them.
A teenager asks why their own village is still hungry. Nobody in the room has studied theology. Everybody in the room knows hunger.

teach.h: BASE COMMUNITIES: THE BIBLE ON THE BENCHES.
teach.b: They were called base communities: small groups of poor Catholics, often led by lay people rather than priests, reading the Bible against their own lives.
In Nicaragua, a priest named Ernesto Cardenal wrote down the conversations of the farmers and fishermen in his island parish, and the book became The Gospel in Solentiname.
One passage from Luke sounds different in rooms like those.

Jesus stands up in the synagogue in his hometown, is handed the book of the prophet Isaiah, and reads, in the King James Bible: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor."
In a tin-roofed chapel, that line doesn't sound like a metaphor. Alongside these groups grew what was called liberation theology, which spoke of God's special care for the poor.

teach.h: A REAL ARGUMENT INSIDE THE CHURCH.
teach.b: It stirred real argument. Supporters said it was simply the Gospel read honestly from the bottom.
Some Catholic leaders, Rome among them, warned against borrowing ideas from Marxism, and the debate was carried on inside the church.

teach.h: A PENTECOSTAL WAVE ON THE SAME BLOCK.
teach.b: Meanwhile a second wave rose in the same neighborhoods: Pentecostal churches, small congregations in rented rooms with guitars, healing prayer and preachers from the block.
The two looked nothing alike, and didn't always get along. But both put the Bible in ordinary hands and asked what it said to people who had very little.
In Matthew, Jesus says it in a prayer: "thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes."

how: Small Bible-sharing groups meet in homes and parishes across Latin America, reading a passage aloud and talking about what it says to their own lives, while Pentecostal congregations gather for lively worship, preaching and prayer for healing.

o: a list of laws for the temple priests.
the Spirit of the Lord is upon me, to preach the gospel to the poor.

games.why: Luke 4:18. read in a poor parish, it sounds like good news addressed to the people in the room.

practice: Say the line from Luke slowly, twice: the Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor.
Then ask the benches' question, what do I hear, not as a scholar would, but about your own street and your own week, and let one honest answer come. If you pray, you can pray the line back.

wordCard.voice: Latin America. Base communities reading scripture together in small, poor parishes, and a Pentecostal wave in the same streets: the Bible in ordinary hands.

orig.note: Greek: to the poor — the word in Luke 4:18, from ptōchos, a poor person.

carryVoice: Your line: the bible read by the poor. Nobody on those benches needed a degree to hear it. That's day nine hundred seventy-nine, done.
